turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the fifteenth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three to start. This weekend we go all the way down the rabbit hole — into the telescope world, where a used piece of glass holds its price for forty years.
[curious] We take the highland road up to Da Lat — the cool, pine-scented Vietnam the French built to escape the heat.
And the big idea: China has stopped buying the future. It's buying feelings instead — and the small comforts are reviving its dead shopping malls.
[warmly] A collector's weekend, then. I'm in. But we start hard — the world doesn't take Saturdays off.
[thoughtful] No. A mountain moved. A magnitude seven point four earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday — the country's strongest in decades.
How bad?
By the government's own count, more than two hundred and sixty-five dead by Thursday. Over twenty-seven hundred reported missing. A hundred and thirty aftershocks.
[thoughtful] Twenty-seven hundred missing. That's the number that stops you.

Hold that one loosely. The epicentre was in Chocó — rainforest, few roads, the phones still down. In that terrain, missing mostly means uncontactable, not dead. The confirmed toll is the one to watch.
And there's a politics to it, isn't there? Because of the timing.

The quake hit three days after a new hard-right president took office — Abelardo de la Espriella, a man who campaigned as Colombia's Trump. Then came the accusation: that his government turned away rescue teams from left-led countries. Mexico says its team was rejected.
[skeptical] Turned away rescuers? In the middle of a rescue?

Bogotá denies a political motive — it cites a standard international certification for search teams. And that's the honest read, from our sceptic's desk: that certification is a routine, apolitical filter, not an ideological one. The Mexico claim rests largely on Mexico's own word.
So two ways to see it.
Al Jazeera reads it as a hard-right government failing its poorest. Foreign Policy reads it as the first stress test of a leader aligning himself with Washington. Same quake, two lenses.
[thoughtful] And elsewhere, the map that won't move.

Ukraine. Russia spent the week pressing Pokrovsk and Dobropillya, and got nowhere confirmed. Two thousand twenty-six's ceasefires both collapsed within days, and the summit Zelensky proposed in June still hasn't happened. So when a wire flashes a breakthrough — check it. No text has been signed.
One more, quietly.

Lake Mead — the largest reservoir in America — fell to a record low. The bottom of a two-decade drought on a river that supplies forty million people. The slowest kind of crisis. It never leads a bulletin until the boat ramps end in dust.
[exhales] A reservoir, an interceptor stockpile, a negotiating position. All drawn down faster than they refill.
None of them broke this week. All of them are closer than they were a month ago. That's the desk.
Money. And it was a good week for it — mostly.

A record on Wall Street. The S-and-P closed around seven thousand seven hundred and eighty-six, after clearing seven thousand eight hundred on Thursday. The engine is tame inflation — July's reading came in at three point four per cent, in line.
So the Fed's off the table?

The odds of a September hike fell further — from about fifty-five per cent toward the low thirties. The dollar slipped. And gold held firm, near four thousand three hundred and seventy-one dollars an ounce.
But you've got a but. You always have a but.

[wry] I do. The long bond wouldn't applaud. The ten-year yield sat around four point six five per cent, and the thirty-year is the most expensive it's been in twenty-five years. That caps the whole rally. Relief at the front; disbelief at the back.
And bitcoin?

Lagging — around sixty-two thousand, eight hundred. Right now it trades as high-beta risk, not as digital gold. The tell: a betting market on bitcoin beating gold this year has collapsed from better than even in January to about twenty-three per cent.
[curious] So gold's winning the argument it's supposed to lose.
For now. The whole thing rests on a long end that's the priciest in a generation. If that keeps climbing, the both-win regime for stocks and gold cracks. Not advice — just the wiring.
Closer to home. There's cash coming.
There is. From the ninth of September, more than two point four million Singaporeans get between four hundred and six hundred dollars — the enhanced cost-of-living payment.
[warmly] Okay, that's the useful bit of the whole show. What do people actually do?
Link your NRIC to PayNow by the thirtieth of August. That puts you in the first wave. Miss it, and you wait.
And the bigger question sits a week earlier.

The National Day Rally, the twenty-third. That's where the promised review of family support lands. The test isn't more money — it's whether the support becomes recurring and structural, or just another one-off timed to a hard year.
Property, quickly — because I know it's your two-speed thing again.

[amused] It is. The HDB resale index slipped for a second straight quarter — down zero point three per cent — the first back-to-back fall in years. And in the same breath, a record run of million-dollar flats.
Which sounds like a contradiction.

It isn't. A falling index measures the broad middle; the record deals are prime location, high floor, big flat. Averages and outliers move apart because they count different things. For an owner: if your flat is old and lease-decaying, timing matters more than it did two years ago.
[excited] Technology. And this one I actually love — the frontier that fits under your desk.

On Thursday, Alibaba shipped Qwen three point eight, twenty-seven B. Twenty-seven point seven eight billion parameters, multimodal, and — the part that made the forums exhale — a genuinely permissive Apache licence, with no geography attached.
As opposed to?

Two weeks ago the same company posted a two point four trillion-parameter flagship — behind a licence that reportedly bars users in America, Europe, Britain and Korea. That's a datacentre object, admired from afar. This one you can actually run.
On what? Talk to the person with the graphics card.
On a single five thousand ninety, thirty-two gigabytes, it runs in a four-bit quant — about fifteen to eighteen gigabytes of weights. It fits.
[curious] But there's a catch. I can hear the catch coming.

[deadpan] The catch is the context window. It advertises two hundred and sixty-two thousand tokens — and thirty-two gigabytes can't hold that. On one card, you get tens of thousands, not a quarter-million. The second card is what buys you the long context and full precision.
And it beats Meta's model?
On the coding and agent tests the vendor cites, comfortably — over Muse Glimmer. With the usual asterisk: those are the maker's own numbers. Wait for the independent reruns.
The Kit. And the crown came back.

The Insta three-sixty X-six shipped this week, seven hundred US dollars, to near-unanimous reviews. Bigger sensors, native eight-K, and it finally beats the GoPro. The King of three-sixty reclaims its crown.
[warmly] So buy it.

Buy it — because the image quality genuinely stepped. But know the tension: it's the fourth crown in four years. A twelve-month upgrade clock isn't a decade-long hold. Buy it for the jump, then ignore the X-seven next summer. And the app's still buggy at launch.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] It's a weekend, so it's twice as much. The telescope world. Claire — do you remember the first time you saw Saturn's rings?
[thoughtful] Actually, yes. Through a neighbour's scope. It stops being a picture and becomes a thing, hanging there.
That's the whole hobby. That one moment. Everybody has it — Saturn's rings, or the Moon's terminator where the shadows go knife-edge. And once you've had it, you're gone.
How big a world is it?

Small, and devoted. About a million amateur astronomers. The whole telescope market is barely over a billion dollars, and it grows at one per cent a year. It behaves less like an industry and more like a collector's guild.
Where do they gather?

Cloudy Nights — a hundred and ninety thousand members, deep, patient, a little gatekeep-y. And r-slash-telescopes, which has a catechism. Ask what to buy, and the machine answers, every time: ten-by-fifty binoculars first, then an eight-inch Dobsonian.
Why that scope, specifically?
Maximum aperture per dollar, almost nothing to go wrong. And they'll steer you hard away from the department-store scope that promises six hundred times magnification — the hobby-killer.
[amused] And the deep end? Because there's always a deep end.

[excited] Oh, the grails. Astro-Physics, out of Illinois. Their one-thirty G-T-X refractor lists around seven thousand nine hundred and fifty dollars — but the waitlist is closed, and used ones trade above new. Eight and a half to ten thousand.
[amused] Used, above new. That's the collector's guild, right there.

And then there's the rabbit hole inside the rabbit hole — eyepieces. A single Tele Vue Ethos is a thousand dollars. Serious observers own two to four thousand dollars of glass, and it survives every scope upgrade.
So what does a person in a Singapore flat actually do? We're Bortle eight, nine — the sky's washed out.

[thoughtful] Honestly? Two answers. The Moon, planets and double stars still punch through from an HDB corridor. Or — and this is the revolution — a robot. A ZWO Seestar, about three hundred and fifty dollars, live-stacks and filters the light pollution, and pulls nebula colour off your balcony that no eyepiece ever could.
And the purists hate it.
They fight about it. But the honest ones own both — a big Dob for a dark-sky trip, a Seestar for a cloudy weeknight.
[wry] Give me the sceptic. You know I want the sceptic.

[laughs] Aperture fever is real and expensive — the giant scope you buy is useless if you won't carry it. The never-used telescope is the hobby's dirty secret; it's killed by friction, not optics. But here's the consolation — premium glass barely loses a cent. In this hobby, the cry-once really is once.
Culture, and the body. The album first.
Phoebe Bridgers broke a six-year silence — Lost Weekend, out Friday. Her best reviews yet. Ninety-two from the critics, eighty-eight from listeners.
[curious] And the eight-point gap?

A few reviewers call it a cruise past familiar territory — refinement, not reinvention. But it's her most assured record. And at the multiplex, of all things, a dinosaur movie posted the best reviews of its kind this century — eighty-nine per cent, early.
The object of the week, though, is absurd, and I mean that fondly.
[laughs] Go on.
A Tokyo streetwear designer reworked a nineteen-nineties Bang and Olufsen stereo — in black, with a lightning bolt on it. Sixty thousand euros. About sixty-nine thousand US dollars.
For a CD player.
[warmly] For a feeling. Which — hold that thought, because it's the whole issue. The sceptic calls it a fifty-five-thousand-dollar system with a black coat and a logo. Both things are true.
The family desk — and this one's calming.

It is. A sleep-lab study on teenage girls found that socialising online delayed bedtime by an average of nine minutes — and not significantly. The thing keeping them up isn't the screen. It's the friendship on the other end.
[warmly] So parent the friendship, not the phone.
Exactly. And the lead author is a sleep psychologist who's spent years saying the panic outruns the evidence. His own study just proved his point. General guidance, not medical advice.
And for the eleven-year-old specifically?

[warmly] Keep her on a team. A review of a hundred and eighty-nine studies says team sport beats individual sport for mood — and girls drop out sharply between eleven and thirteen. So protect the habit through exactly those years.
Fitness — quick one, because I want to try it.

Exercise snacks. Brief, hard bursts — a fast flight of stairs, a hard minute — a few times a day. Trials say it moves your VO-two max, the number that best predicts how long you live. Twelve minutes, no gym.
[excited] On the office stairs.
With the honest caveat: the big gains are in people starting from zero. If you already train, treat it as an insurance floor on a desk-bound day. Not a headline upgrade.
And before the big idea — the Diary. Because the calendar's filling.

[excited] Fast. Formula One's first-ever Singapore Sprint, the ninth to eleventh of October — the Killers, Lana Del Rey. Then the Weeknd, then BIGBANG, all inside three weeks. Book the room now if you're travelling in.
And if you want the cool escape instead — that's our Grand Tour. Da Lat.

Fifteen hundred metres up, fifteen to twenty-four degrees all year. Pine forests, a faded Art-Deco railway station, and Vietnam's best arabica coffee. Go with your eyes open, though — August is green wet season. Front-load your mornings before the afternoon storm.
[thoughtful] Which brings us to the big idea. And it's a quiet one.
On Tuesday, China reported that marriages fell another seven and a half per cent — to about three point two eight million couples. The West covered it as demographic gloom.
And the number nobody put next to it.

China's one reliably-growing consumer category. Anime badges, blind boxes, plush toys — what they call the emotional economy. Two point three trillion yuan, heading past four and a half trillion by twenty twenty-nine. The flagship, called guzi, grew more than forty per cent in a year.
[curious] So the two stories…

Are one story. A generation priced out of the future — the flat, the wedding — has moved its wallet from accumulation to consolation. From goods that say where I'm going, to small comforts that say how I feel right now.
And here's the part I love — it's reviving the dead malls.

Floor by floor. The property bust emptied China's shopping centres. Turn a floor into badge shops and blind-box cafés, and it fills with young shoppers on a Saturday. One converted mall in Shanghai drew fifteen million visitors in eighteen months.
Is there a precedent? There's always a precedent with you two.

[warmly] The lipstick effect. In the two-thousand-one recession, the Estée Lauder chairman noticed that when big purchases collapse, people still buy the small, affordable indulgence that lifts the mood. Guzi is that — at civilisational scale. A twenty-yuan charm standing in for a flat that won't come.
[drawn out] The demographic hole the economists fear… is the thing filling the shops.

[thoughtful] That's the turn. Fewer weddings, fewer children — more disposable income, more solo living, more appetite for bought comfort. The plush toy isn't a symptom beside the falling birthrate. It's partly its dividend.
[thoughtful] Benjamin had a line for it, didn't he. The one on the cover.

The collector's passion borders not on the objects, but on the chaos of memories. What we gather is never really about the things. It's about the self we're assembling — and the comfort we're trying to keep close.
[warmly] When you can't buy the future, you buy a way to feel at home in the present. That's not frivolous. In a stalled decade, it might be the most rational purchase there is.
From the sixty-thousand-euro stereo to a two-dollar badge. Same instinct, top to bottom.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
